newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - ABARE boosts forecast Australian sugar crop.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - ABARE boosts forecast Australian sugar crop.

text.p: Official Australian forecaster the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics has increased its forecast of Australian sugar production to 5.5 million tonnes in 1996/97 (September to August) from its previous forecast of 5.1 million tonnes.

Production at the latest forecast level would be up by 9.7 percent on 1995/96, ABARE said. "The significant increase can be attributed mainly to improved rainfall and an increase in area planted, including the establishment of sugar production in the Ord River region of Western Australia," it said.
Australian sugar exports are forecast to rise by 7.9 percent to 4.30 million tonnes in 1996/97, ABARE said in its latest forecast. This is down on the previous forecast of 4.39 million.
However, a stronger Australian dollar and lower world sugar prices mean that average returns to Australian producers are forecast to fall by 7.5 percent in 1996/97, ABARE said.
World sugar prices are forecast to fall by 11 percent to US10.8 cents/lb in 1996/97, ABARE said.
This compares with the previous ABARE forecast of world prices of US10.4 cents/lb.
The fall is less than would be expected given the high level of total sugar stocks and the stocks-to-use ratio, ABARE said.
However, about 60 percent of the surplus was low quality sugar in India, which was unlikely to have a significant impact on world sugar prices, it said.
Additionally, the lack of suitable infrastructure in major producing countries such as Brazil and Thailand has led to some exporting difficulties for those countries, it said.

World sugar consumption is expected to continue to rise in 1996/97. The main focus of this growth would be in Asia, reflecting strong economic growth and changing tastes which had translated to raid expansion in demand, it said.
World sugar production is forecast to be slightly less than the record 122 million tonnes produced in 1995/96, it said.

The fall is expected to result from lower production in India, following record production in 1995/96 and a likely decrease in prices paid to Indian producers. The falls are expected to more than offset forecast increases in production in Brazil, Australia, South Africa and Thailand, it said.
